questions.question: Hexane boils at 68,7 °C, 2-methylpentane at 60,3 °C and 2,2-dimethylbutane at 49,7 °C, yet all three share the molecular formula C₆H₁₄. Explain the trend fully, using the four-step structure for property explanations.
questions.expected_answer: Step one, structural difference: the three compounds are chain isomers differing only in branching — hexane is unbranched, 2-methylpentane carries one methyl branch, and 2,2-dimethylbutane carries two branches on the same carbon and is the most compact. Step two, forces: all three are nonpolar alkanes, so the only intermolecular forces present are London (dispersion) forces. Step three, comparison: London forces act over the surface of contact between neighbouring molecules. Straight hexane chains can lie alongside one another and attract along their whole length; branching pulls the molecule into a compact, nearly spherical shape that touches its neighbours over a much smaller area, so the dispersion forces weaken as branching increases. Step four, energy: weaker intermolecular forces need less energy to overcome, so the boiling point falls as branching increases — from 68,7 °C for the straight chain down to 49,7 °C for the most branched isomer. Molar mass explains nothing here, since all three isomers have identical formulae and masses — the shape alone changes the contact, and the contact changes the grip.

questions.question: Pentane (M = 72 g·mol⁻¹, boiling point 36,1 °C), butanal (M = 72 g·mol⁻¹, boiling point 74,8 °C) and butan-1-ol (M = 74 g·mol⁻¹, boiling point 117,7 °C) have nearly equal molar masses. Explain the boiling point differences, and predict with a reason where butanoic acid would fit.
questions.expected_answer: Because the molar masses are nearly equal, the London forces in the three compounds are of similar strength, so the differences must come from the functional groups. Pentane is a nonpolar alkane with only London forces between its molecules — the weakest total attraction and the lowest boiling point. Butanal is an aldehyde: its carbonyl group gives the molecule a permanent dipole, so dipole-dipole forces act in addition to the London forces; the stronger total attraction needs more energy to overcome, lifting the boiling point to 74,8 °C. Butan-1-ol is an alcohol: its OH group has hydrogen bonded directly to oxygen, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds — the strongest intermolecular force in this topic — and the boiling point climbs to 117,7 °C. Butanoic acid would boil higher than all three (in fact at about 163,5 °C): its carboxyl group can hydrogen-bond at two sites, and pairs of acid molecules clamp together as dimers held by a double hydrogen bond, giving the strongest total intermolecular attraction of the four and therefore demanding the most energy to separate the molecules.

questions.question: Define vapour pressure, state its relationship to intermolecular force strength and boiling point, and use it to explain why an ester's fruity smell fills a room while butan-1-ol evaporates only slowly from an open beaker.
questions.expected_answer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour of a liquid that is in equilibrium with the liquid in a closed container. It runs opposite to intermolecular force strength: strong intermolecular forces hold molecules inside the liquid so few escape, giving a low vapour pressure and a high boiling point; weak intermolecular forces let many molecules escape, giving a high vapour pressure and a low boiling point — a volatile liquid. A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the atmospheric pressure above it. Esters experience London and dipole-dipole forces but cannot hydrogen-bond with one another, so their intermolecular forces are comparatively weak; their vapour pressure is relatively high, large numbers of molecules escape into the air, and those airborne molecules carry the fruity smell to your nose — the very property that makes esters useful in flavourings and perfumes. Butan-1-ol's molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds, the strongest intermolecular force in the syllabus, so far fewer molecules escape per second: its vapour pressure is lower, its evaporation slower, and its boiling point higher.
